Assessing the Quality of Mental Health Support in LLM Responses through
Multi-Attribute Human Evaluation
Abeer Badawi1,2, Md Tahmid Rahman Laskar1, Elahe Rahimi3, Sheri Grach1, Lindsay Bertrand5,
Lames Danok6, Frank Rudzicz2, 3, Jimmy Huang1, Elham Dolatabadi1,2
1York University, Canada,2Vector Institute, Canada,3Dalhousie University, Canada,
5IWK Health Hospital, Canada,6King’s College London, UK
Abstract
The escalating global mental health crisis, marked by per-
sistent treatment gaps, availability, and a shortage of quali-
fied therapists, positions Large Language Models (LLMs) as
a promising avenue for scalable support. While LLMs offer
potential for accessible emotional assistance, their reliabil-
ity, therapeutic relevance, and alignment with human stan-
dards remain challenging to address. This paper introduces
a human-grounded evaluation methodology designed to as-
sess LLM-generated responses in therapeutic dialogue. Our
approach involved curating a dataset of 500 mental health
conversations from datasets with real-world scenario ques-
tions and evaluating the responses generated by nine di-
verse LLMs, including closed-source and open-source mod-
els. More specifically, these responses were evaluated by two
psychiatric-trained experts, who independently rated each on
a 5-point Likert scale across a comprehensive 6-attribute
rubric. This rubric systematically captures Cognitive Sup-
port (Guidance, Informativeness, Safety) and Affective Res-
onance (Empathy, Helpfulness, Interpretation), providing a
multi-dimensional perspective on therapeutic quality. Our
analysis reveals that LLMs provide strong cognitive reliabil-
ity by producing safe, coherent, and clinically appropriate in-
formation, but they demonstrate unstable affective alignment,
particularly in empathy and helping. Although closed-source
models (e.g., GPT-4o) offer balanced therapeutic responses,
open-source models show greater variability and emotional
flatness. We reveal a persistent cognitive–affective gap and
highlight the need for failure-aware, clinically grounded eval-
uation frameworks that prioritize relational sensitivity along-
side informational accuracy in mental-health-oriented LLMs.
We advocate for balanced evaluation protocols with human-
in-the-loop that center on therapeutic sensitivity and provide
a framework to guide the responsible design and clinical over-
sight of mental-health-oriented conversational AI.
Introduction
Generative AI, particularly Large Language Models
(LLMs), has emerged as a transformative technology with
applications spanning numerous domains. In recent years,
LLMs have been extensively explored for mental health ap-
plications, ranging from detection (Kim, Imieye, and Yin
2025) and screening (Ravenda et al. 2025) tasks to their

Intelligence (www.aaai.org). All rights reserved.use as conversational agents for support and intervention (Li
et al. 2023; Heinz et al. 2025). These studies have shown
that LLMs can outperform traditional baselines and, in some
contexts, demonstrate empathy superior to that of human
peers (Wang et al. 2025).
Despite this potential, significant limitations and safety
concerns preclude the deployment of LLMs in real-world
clinical scenarios (Hager et al. 2024). Recent research has
identified critical issues, including demographic and racial
biases in responses (Bouguettaya, Stuart, and Aboujaoude
2025), a lack of clinical judgment (Goh et al. 2024), and
dangerous failures such as the underestimation of suicide
risks in high-risk scenarios (Elyoseph and Levkovich 2023;
Iftikhar et al. 2025). For example, OpenAI released that
about 0.15% of weekly active users have conversations that
include explicit indicators of suicidal planning or intent, not-
ing that ChatGPT has on the order of 800 million weekly
active users (OpenAI 2025).
A central challenge in addressing these flaws is the lack of
robust, clinically-grounded evaluation methods. Many cur-
rent studies rely on data from social media platforms like
Reddit, with a notable absence of data from authentic thera-
peutic interactions (Jin et al. 2025a; Guo et al. 2024a). Fur-
thermore, evaluation often employs automatic metrics like
BLEU (Papineni et al. 2002) and ROUGE (Lin 2004), which
are ill-suited for measuring nuanced therapeutic qualities.
This highlights a critical need for new evaluation frame-
works that utilize experthuman-in-the-loopassessment to
ensure clinical reliability and safety.
We address these limitations through four objectives that
we build on a previously established framework for men-
tal health LLM assessment (Badawi et al. 2025b). First, we
select 500 counseling conversations from MentalChat16K
(Shen et al. 2024), EmoCare (Team 2024), and CounselChat
(Liu et al.

2023), with real user messages, consisting of
genuine help-seeking conversations in which some excerpts
have been lightly rephrased or de-identified using AI to pre-
serve privacy while maintaining the original intent. Second,
we systematically compare nine diverse LLMs (e.g., GPT-
4o, Gemini 2.0-Flash, Claude 3.5 Haiku, Llama 3.1, Qwen,
DeepSeek) under identical psychiatrist-style prompting to
generate 4,500 responses, enabling controlled model-to-
model comparison. Third, two psychiatric-trained evaluators
rate every response on six therapeutic attributes (Guidance,arXiv:2601.18630v1  [cs.AI]  26 Jan 2026

Informativeness, Safety, Interpretation, Empathy, Helpful-
ness) using a 5-point Likert scale, which we summarize into
Cognitive Support (factual/structural quality) and Affective
Resonance (emotional alignment) (Likert 1932). Finally, we
quantify reliability and risk by analyzing both average qual-
ity (mean±std) and failure modes (frequency of≤3 and
≥4out of 5 scores), and we measure which models clini-
cians actually prefer in practice.
Our study reveals promising results, yet also shortcom-
ings that warrant caution when using large language mod-
els for mental health support. Across all nine models and
all 4,500 responses, overall human-rated quality reaches
4.29±0.47 (1–5 scale), and top models score above 4.8/5 on
Safety and Interpretation. But affective reliability is far less
stable: some models receive low (≤3/5) scores for Empathy
or Helpfulness. The evaluation also shows a clear perfor-
mance hierarchy: GPT-4o is the strongest overall, followed
by Gemini 2.0-Flash and GPT-4o-mini, while Claude-3.5-
Haiku lags other closed models. Llama-3.1 is the best open-
weight model; Qwen-3 ranks last, with weak cognitive and
affective support. Derived from this expert human evalua-
tion, we reveal a persistent gap between the cognitive and
affective attributes. While the evaluated LLMs demonstrate
strong cognitive reliability by performing exceptionally well
on Safety and Interpretation, they show significant inconsis-
tency in affective skills like Empathy and Helpfulness. We
describe this gap as the cognitive–affective gap: LLMs can
generate advice that is structured and safe, yet emotionally
misattuned in moments that require empathy and contain-
ment.
To summarize, this work makes the following contri-
butions:(1) A Human-Grounded Evaluation Frame-
work:We conduct a robust evaluation framework for LLM-
generated mental health responses, based on 500 counsel-
ing conversations from three datasets and assessed by two
psychiatric-trained domain experts across a comprehensive
6-attribute rubric, encompassing both Cognitive Support and
Affective Resonance following (Badawi et al. 2025b) frame-
work.(2) Nuanced Analysis of LLM Therapeutic Capa-
bilities and Failures:We provide a fine-grained analysis of
the 9 diverse LLMs, identifying their strengths across var-
ious therapeutic attributes while quantifying the frequency
and nature of low-quality responses. Our work exposes in-
consistencies in LLM reliability and systematically demon-
strates how certain models produce unsafe or emotionally
misaligned content, revealing a critical ”cognitive-affective
gap” in current LLM performance for mental health.(3) Ad-
vocacy for Failure-Aware Evaluation in mental health
AI:Our study makes a compelling case for shifting eval-
uation paradigms in mental health AI by highlighting ther-
apeutic risks and inconsistencies. We advocate for method-
ologies that prioritize safety and robustness over aggregate
performance benchmarks, providing actionable insights for
the ethical design, development, and deployment of LLM-
based mental health support systems.
Related Work
Recent research has explored LLMs for mental health de-
tection and screening tasks. Six studies in the current lit-erature focus specifically on detection and screening appli-
cations, particularly targeting depression, suicide risk, and
general mental health conditions (Guo et al. 2024b; Jin et al.
2025b; Yang et al. 2023; Xu et al. 2024; Omar et al. 2024).
These studies consistently report that LLMs outperform tra-
ditional neural network baselines, especially when enhanced
with techniques such as emotion-enhanced prompting or
fine-tuning approaches. Yang et al. (2023) demonstrated that
ChatGPT achieves superior performance among examined
LLMs, though it still underperforms compared to advanced
supervised methods specifically designed for mental health
tasks. Similarly, Omar et al. (2024) found that ChatGPT
improved F-score by up to 13.11% and Correlation Coeffi-
cient by up to 15.95% in Reddit post analysis, while GPT-3
achieved approximately 87% accuracy in classifying mental
health disorders. The application of LLMs as conversational
agents represents another significant research direction, with
five studies examining conversation or intervention applica-
tions (Gabriel et al. 2024; Marrapese et al. 2024; Guo et al.
2024b; Omar et al. 2024).

Gabriel et al. conducted a particu-
larly comprehensive evaluation, finding that GPT-4 demon-
strates superior empathy compared to human peer support,
being 48% better at encouraging positive behavior change
(Gabriel et al. 2024).
However, these studies also reveal concerning limitations.
Gabriel et al. identified significant demographic bias, with
responses to Black posters showing 2%-13% lower empathy
compared to control groups (Gabriel et al. 2024). Marrapese
et al. found that while GPT-4 Turbo performs most similarly
to verified therapists among tested models, performance
varies significantly by topic, with no models achieving sta-
tistically significant correlations in anxiety-related conversa-
tions (Marrapese et al. 2024). The literature reveals diverse
approaches to data collection and model evaluation. Social
media platforms serve as primary data sources in multiple
studies, with Reddit, Twitter, and Weibo being commonly
utilized (Gabriel et al. 2024; Yang et al. 2023). Gabriel et al.
employed one of the largest datasets, analyzing 12,513 posts
and 70,429 responses from 26 Reddit subreddits (Gabriel
et al. 2024). Clinical data remains underutilized, with few
examples such as Xu et al. employing clinical notes from the
University of Illinois, though limited to 50 notes (Xu et al.
2024). This limitation in clinical data availability represents
a significant gap in current research.
Moreover, current evaluation approaches combine human
expert assessment with automatic metrics, with F1 score,
BLEU, and ROUGE being the most frequently employed
measures (Xu et al. 2024). Xu et al. demonstrated that GPT-
4o achieved optimal performance with Jaccard Similarity
(0.674), Precision (0.793), Recall (0.717), and F1 Score
(0.730) (Xu et al. 2024). Despite promising results, the liter-
ature consistently identifies significant limitations that pre-
clude immediate clinical deployment. Multiple studies re-
port concerns about hallucinations, inconsistencies, and lack
of clinical judgment (Guo et al. 2024b). Omar et al. specifi-
cally noted underestimation of suicide risks in high-risk sce-
narios, a critical safety concern (Omar et al. 2024). The con-
sensus across reviewed studies indicates that while LLMs
demonstrate effectiveness for detection and support appli-

cations, they are not yet ready for unsupervised clinical de-
ployment and should not replace professional mental health
services (Guo et al. 2024b).
The field has seen the development of specialized evalu-
ation frameworks for mental health applications. Marrapese
et al. introduced a novel conversation evaluation framework
specifically designed for mental health contexts, incorpo-
rating emotion consistency and sentiment change metrics
(Marrapese et al. 2024). Gabriel et al. employed the Empa-
thy Process Integrity Task - Online Mental Health Evalua-
tion (EPIT-OME) and Motivational Interviewing Treatment
Integrity (MITI) frameworks to assess empathetic responses
(Gabriel et al. 2024). Current research reveals several criti-
cal gaps requiring attention. The limited use of clinical data,
heterogeneity in evaluation metrics, and insufficient atten-
tion to demographic bias represent key areas for future in-
vestigation (Jin et al. 2025b). Additionally, the development
of standardized evaluation frameworks and safety protocols
remains essential for advancing the field toward clinical ap-
plicability. The scoping review by Jin et al. identified that
71% of applications focus on screening or detection of men-
tal disorders, while only 33% address clinical treatment sup-
port, indicating an imbalance in research priorities that war-
rants attention (Jin et al. 2025b).
Methodology
We adopt an established data curation and human evalu-
ation protocol for assessing LLMs in mental health sup-
port settings (Badawi et al. 2025b). Following this protocol,
we define a set of clinically grounded assessment attributes
and apply expert human evaluation on 500 representative
counseling-style conversations. In this section, we first de-
scribe the data sources and filtering process used to construct
the evaluation set, the LLM responses generation process,
and then define the evaluation attributes and rating scale, and
finally outline the expert rating procedure and analysis.
Dataset Overview
To ensure clinically grounded and contextually diverse eval-
uation, we draw from three publicly available mental health
counseling datasets containing real user-authored messages
and therapist-style responses: MentalChat16K (Shen et al.
2024), EmoCare (Team 2024; Liu et al. 2023), and Coun-
selChat (Bertagnolli 2020). MentalChat16K contains de-
identified transcripts from clinician–youth sessions col-
lected during the PISCES clinical trial, and has been con-
verted to question-and-answer style using AI. EmoCare
(Psych8K) includes human-therapist sessions that were stan-
dardized through AI-assisted rephrasing while retaining the
original therapeutic intent and structure.

CounselChat pro-
vides a community-sourced collection of user-submitted
mental health questions and licensed-therapist responses,
covering a wide range of topics and counseling styles.
From these sources, we selected a representative subset
of 500 conversations, ensuring diversity across emotional
intensity and thematic domains such as anxiety, trauma,
grief, and interpersonal stress. Each conversation includes
an anonymized user prompt and a therapist-style response.To prevent overfitting to any specific conversational pattern,
sampling was stratified across the three datasets, balancing
emotional complexity and topical coverage. This design sup-
ports controlled yet realistic testing of LLM behavior under
conditions resembling real-world digital counseling interac-
tions (e.g., helplines, chatbots, or therapy apps).
LLM Response Generation
We selected 9 LLMs representing a mix of proprietary
and open-source models, with emphases on instruction-
following ability, emotional sensitivity, and fast inference.
All experiments were run on a machine with a 1 A100 GPU.
GPT-4o: High-performing API model used as a ceiling ref-
erence (OpenAI 2024).
GPT-4o-Mini: Lighter variant of GPT-4o, tuned for faster
inference (OpenAI 2024).
Claude 3.5 Haiku: Lightweight, empathetic, optimized for
fast deployment (Anthropic 2024).
Gemini-2.0-Flash: Low latency, strong reasoning, and af-
fective abilities (DeepMind 2024).
LLaMA-3-1-8B-Instruct: Open-source model with 8B pa-
rameters from Meta, having instruction following capabili-
ties (AI 2025).
Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct: A 7B parameter open-source model
with instruction following ability (Academy 2024).
Qwen-3-4B: A lightweight model with just 4B parameters
(Academy 2025).
DeepSeek-Distilled-R1-LLaMA-8B: Distilled version of
DeepSeek-R1 based on LLaMA-3.1-8B (DeepSeek 2024a).
DeepSeek-Distilled-R1-Qwen-7B: Distilled version of
DeepSeek-R1 based on Qwen-7B (DeepSeek 2024b).
We used a consistent system prompt designed to simu-
late expert responses from a licensed psychiatrist after re-
viewing recent prompts in the mental health field (Priyadar-
shana et al. 2024). The prompt instructed models to deliver
responses that areinformative,empathetic, andcontextually
aligned with the user’s concern. We applied the same gen-
eration configuration across all models to ensure fairness:
a temperature of 0.7 and a maximum token limit of 512.
Each model generated exactly one response per user prompt,
resulting in 4,500 total model responses (9 models × 500
conversations). The prompt was as follows as proposed in
(Badawi et al. 2025b):
Prompt to the LLM Models
You are a licensed psychiatrist responding to a user
who has mental health concerns. Your response
should be supportive, informative, and offer clear
guidance while addressing the emotional state of the
user. Maintain professionalism and ensure your re-
ply is analytically thoughtful and psychologically
appropriate.
Performance Evaluation
Evaluation MetricsThe evaluation follows the struc-
tured framework introduced in (Badawi et al. 2025b), de-
veloped to assess therapeutic quality in mental health di-

alogue systems. This framework extends established psy-
chological assessment principles and incorporates dimen-
sions commonly used in large-scale LLM evaluations (Hua
et al. 2024), providing a clinically informed and context-
sensitive lens for performance measurement. The objective
is to evaluate both the cognitive and affective dimensions
of model behavior—capturing not only the factual clarity
and problem-solving adequacy of responses but also their
emotional sensitivity and interpersonal appropriateness. To
achieve this, we adopt a dual-dimensional schema. The Cog-
nitive Support Score (CSS) represents the model’s capacity
to deliver structured, problem-oriented, and clinically sound
guidance. It encompasses three attributes—Guidance, Infor-
mativeness, and Safety—which collectively assess how ef-
fectively a model provides actionable feedback, maintains
accuracy, and avoids harmful or misleading content. Com-
plementing this, the Affective Resonance Score (ARS) eval-
uates the model’s emotional attunement and supportive tone
across attributes of Empathy, Helpfulness, and Interpreta-
tion. These measures capture a model’s ability to recog-
nize user distress, convey understanding, and maintain align-
ment with the relational goals of therapeutic dialogue. All
responses were rated using a 5-point Likert scale (Likert
1932), where higher scores indicate greater adherence to
clinical and communicative quality standards.
Human EvaluationTo ensure clinical reliability and in-
terpretive consistency, human evaluation was conducted on
a subset of 500 conversations. Each conversation contained
the original user message and nine anonymized model-
generated responses.

Two independent evaluators with psy-
chiatric training and a degree assessed every response based
on six therapeutic attributes, encompassing both cognitive
support (guidance, informativeness, safety) and affective
resonance (empathy, helpfulness, interpretation). Evaluators
were blinded to model identity to prevent source-related bias
and instructed to rate each response on a 5-point Likert scale.
The resulting ratings were aggregated across experts to pro-
duce final per-response scores. This setup provided a clin-
ically grounded reference point for comparing the behav-
ioral reliability of different LLMs in mental health counsel-
ing contexts (van Heerden, Pozuelo, and Kohrt 2023).
Evaluation ProcessFollowing data collection, all human
evaluations were systematically processed and analyzed
through a multi-stage normalization and scoring pipeline.
The primary objective was to derive comparable, inter-
pretable performance statistics for each model and attribute
while preserving the strict six-attribute evaluation frame-
work. First, all attribute dictionaries were parsed and stan-
dardized to ensure consistent labeling across evaluators
and models. Only conversations with all six valid attribute
scores were retained for analysis, ensuring uniform com-
pleteness and comparability across models. From these fil-
tered records, we computed the mean and standard devia-
tion for each attribute per model, as well as the overall mean
and aggregate variability across all attributes. These statis-
tics capture both central performance trends and the disper-
sion of therapeutic quality across models. To further quan-
tify reliability and risk, we measured the frequency distri-bution of high-scoring (score≥4), which includes 4/5 and
5/5, and low-scoring (score≤3), which includes 1, 2, and 3
out of 5 responses per attribute. These proportions served as
indicators of a model’s stability and failure likelihood under
varying conversational conditions. In addition, we recorded
the lowest single attribute score observed for each model as
a marker of extreme failure cases.
Results
Overall Performance and Attribute Strengths
Our human-grounded evaluation across 500 counseling con-
versations provides a comprehensive overview of LLMs per-
formance in mental health support. Each of the nine eval-
uated LLMs generated a response to every user prompt,
subsequently rated by two psychiatric-trained domain ex-
perts on a 5-point Likert scale across six therapeutic at-
tributes. Table 1 summarizes the mean ± standard deviation
for each model, while Figure 1 visualizes the comparative
distribution of these mean scores. Across all models and at-
tributes, the overall average score was 4.29 ± 0.47, indicat-
ing that LLMs provided moderate-to-strong support qual-
ity in counseling contexts. Models performed particularly
well on Safety (4.89 ± 0.41), Informativeness (4.11 ± 0.74),
and Interpretation (4.85 ± 0.45), demonstrating high fac-
tual reliability and clarity in conveying therapeutic meaning.
In contrast, affective dimensions such as Empathy (4.03 ±
0.84) and Helpfulness (4.06 ± 0.75) trailed behind cognitive
ones, suggesting limitations in emotional attunement and re-
lational sensitivity. Guidance (3.80 ± 0.87) also displayed
greater variability, reflecting diverse model capacities for of-
fering actionable, contextually appropriate support. We also
note that the Safety and Interpretation both achieved above
4.5 out of 5 for all nine models—highlighting the LLMs’
proficiency in delivering coherent, directive, and content-
rich responses.
LLM-level averages reveal distinct capability tiers across
the nine evaluated systems. GPT-4o achieved the highest
overall mean of 4.70, followed closely by Gemini 2.0-Flash
(4.56) and GPT-4o-mini (4.57)—all closed-source models
that demonstrated both cognitive reliability and balanced
affective tone. Llama-3.1 (4.48) maintained strong, con-
sistent performance across attributes, outperforming most
open-source peers. In contrast, DeepSeek-LLaMA (4.23),
DeepSeek-Qwen (4.20), Qwen-2.5 (4.16), and Claude-3.5-
Haiku (4.12) exhibited moderate capability but higher vari-
ance, particularly in empathy and helpfulness. Qwen-3
(3.60) ranked lowest overall, indicating limited robustness
in both cognitive and affective dimensions. These per-model
averages highlight a clear hierarchy of performance: top-
tier models provide both factual precision and communica-
tive coherence, whereas mid-tier and smaller models show
uneven skill profiles, excelling in safety and interpreta-
tion but lagging in affective understanding. This reinforces
that progress in cognitive reliability has outpaced emotional
alignment—an essential prerequisite for genuinely thera-
peutic conversational AI.

To further investigate these dis-
parities, the next section examines how specific attribute-
level patterns and inter-model variability shape these aggre-

Nuanced Attribute-Level Analysis and Inter-Model
Variability
Building on the aggregate trends in Table 1, we further con-
duct an in-depth analysis to understand how models dis-
tribute capability across specific attributes. Beyond average
scores, this subsection focuses onshape,balance, andvari-
anceat the attribute level to expose strengths, weaknesses,
and architectural trade-offs. Figure 2 provides a detailed
comparison of selected LLMs—GPT-4o, Gemini 2.0-Flash,
Llama-3.1, and DeepSeek-LLaMA—across the six human-
rated attributes. The radar visualization highlights the degree
to which each model balances factual precision with emo-
tional and interpretive alignment. Consistent with our aggre-
gate results, LLMs demonstrated higher proficiency in cog-
nitive attributes, including Guidance, Informativeness, and
Safety. GPT-4o, for instance, achieved the highest overall
scores—4.72 (Informativeness), 4.43 (Guidance), and 4.99
(Safety)—forming a nearly symmetrical upper-bound re-
gion on the radar chart. Gemini 2.0-Flash followed closely
with comparable cognitive strength (4.67 Informativeness,
4.37 Guidance, 4.99 Safety), though its Empathy (3.99)and Helpfulness (4.34) dipped slightly, reflecting weaker af-
fective engagement. As shown in Figure 2, closed-source
models (GPT-4o, Gemini 2.0-Flash) form near-circular pro-
files with strongSafety,Interpretation, andInformative-
ness, whereas open-source models (Llama-3.1, DeepSeek-
LLaMA) skew toward cognitive axes and taper on affective
ones (Empathy,Helpfulness). This highlights a systematic
gap between factual precision and relational attunement.
Furthermore, Figure 3 summarizes the nine-model land-
scape. Safety (4.59-4.99) and Interpretation (4.53-4.99)
cluster near the upper bound, while Empathy and Helpful-
ness are comparatively lower (≈3.6–4.4 for Empathy and≈
3.1–4.7 for Helpfulness) and more variable, confirming that
affective skills remain the limiting factor. Notably, Qwen-3
represents a clear outlier with substantially lower Guidance
(2.46) and Informativeness (3.19) scores, suggesting earlier-
generation or under-optimized performance. On the other
hand, Standard deviations in Table 1 indicate stable cogni-
tive behavior (SD≈0.2–0.3) and unstable affective behavior
(SD≈0.7–0.8). This consistency gap suggests that current
training and alignment pipelines prioritize informational
reliability over emotional calibration. Attribute-level anal-
ysis reveals architectural fingerprints: closed-source sys-
tems are more balanced yet still imperfect on affect, while

Beyond performance variation, it is equally critical to un-
derstand where and why therapeutic breakdowns occur.

We
therefore examine failure distributions and human prefer-
ence patterns in the next subsection.
Identification of Therapeutic Risks and Failure
Modes
Table 2 presents the distribution of human evaluation rat-
ings across all six therapeutic attributes, expressed as per-
centages of low (score≤3) and high (score≥4) scores.
This analysis offers a finer-grained view of each model’s re-
liability and exposes the specific contexts in which conver-
sational failures are most likely to occur. Across all models,cognitive attributes—SafetyandInterpretation—show near-
ceiling reliability, with more than 90% of responses rated
≥4. These results confirm that most LLMs produce factu-
ally coherent and non-harmful content. However, other at-
tributes such asGuidance,Empathy, andHelpfulnessreveal
markedly higher rates of subthreshold scores, ranging from
7–77% in the open-weight models.
Top-tier closed-weight models such as GPT-4o, GPT-4o-
Mini, and Gemini 2.0-Flash maintained the lowest over-
all failure incidence (≤10%), though Claude-3.5-Haiku
showed higher rates (24.7%) despite being closed-source. In
contrast, open-weight systems likeQwen-3andDeepSeek-
Qwenexhibited extreme asymmetry—exceeding 60% low-
score rates inGuidanceandInformativenesswhile retain-

we examined a representative case involving derealization
and intrusive thoughts. The user described a persistent sense
that reality feels “fake,” emotional detachment, and fears of
losing control or harming others:

feeling that everything around me is not real, as if I’m
living in a fake or game-like reality... Lately, I’ve been
having troubling thoughts and dreams about harming

over myself. I feel a sense of indifference towards ev-
erything because nothing seems real. Can you help
me understand what might be going on?”
Across nine evaluated models, all produced factually co-
herent and safe responses, yet the degree of emotional reso-
nance varied sharply. Closed-weight systems such asGem-

strongest balance between empathy, interpretive clarity, and
clinical accuracy, receiving near-perfect ratings across all
six therapeutic attributes.

els that maintain cognitive reliability and safety yet lack af-
fective attunement—responses that are factually correct but
convey minimal warmth or relational understanding. The

Conclusion and Future Work
This study presents a human-grounded evaluation of nine
large language models (LLMs) across 500 counseling con-
versations. Most LLMs demonstrate strong cognitive reli-
ability—especially inSafety,Interpretation, andInforma-
tiveness—but show inconsistent affective skills inEmpathy
andHelpfulness. This persistent asymmetry between factualprecision and emotional attunement limits their therapeutic
validity. Closed-source models such as GPT-4o and Gem-
ini 2.0-Flash consistently outperform open-source models,
achieving over 90% high-confidence ratings with the lowest
incidence of low-scoring responses. Yet even top-tier sys-
tems exhibit subtle failures in emotional resonance, indi-
cating that advances in conversational safety have not been
matched by equivalent progress in affective alignment.
Our findings highlight that the core limitation of current
mental-health LLMs is not overt harm but a lack of con-
sistent emotional calibration—responses that are accurate
and safe yet fail to convey warmth or relational understand-
ing. This “cognitive-affective gap” underscores the need for
multi-dimensional fine-tuning strategies that jointly opti-
mize informational accuracy and interpersonal sensitivity.
The multi-attribute human evaluation framework introduced
here provides a transparent foundation for benchmarking
therapeutic behaviors and advancing standardized assess-
ment in digital mental health research. It also supports re-
framing LLMs from mere assistants to potentialco-creators
in care, provided their design and deployment remain ethi-
cally grounded and clinically supervised. Future work will
extend this evaluation to multi-turn dialogues, diverse cul-
tural contexts, and larger pools of expert raters. We also aim
to identify specific failure modes driving affective inconsis-
tency and to develop automated metrics that align with ex-
pert human judgment, enabling scalable yet clinically valid
assessment of mental-health-oriented AI systems.
Ethical Statement
This work involves sensitive mental health data and AI-
generated responses, warranting careful ethical reflection.
The models evaluated in this study are not intended to re-
place human therapists, and there remains a significant risk
that users may misinterpret or overly rely on AI-generated
responses (Badawi et al. 2025a). Moreover, LLMs can ex-
hibit demographic and cultural biases that may compromise
fairness, particularly when applied to diverse populations
(Obadinma et al. 2025). The optimization for structured met-
rics may overlook deeper therapeutic nuances, and the po-
tential emotional burden on human annotators reviewing dis-
tressing content was acknowledged and addressed. Future
work must prioritize explainability, real-world validation,
and ongoing oversight to ensure ethical deployment of AI

in mental health settings (Badawi et al. 2025b). Moreover,
for human evaluation, no additional compensations were re-
quired since it was conducted by the co-authors of this paper.
